---

Imagine writing an app once, in a language that reads like Python.

It opens as a real app on Linux, in the browser, on Android, on a Mac and on an iPhone. Each one uses that platform's own buttons, menus and text fields, not an imitation of them. The heavy lifting, a million rows summed, sorted or charted, runs on the GPU, in the same language and the same file. And when an AI agent wants to use the app, it doesn't scrape pixels or guess at buttons. The app is already a set of tools the agent can call.

That's **omxcode**. Its showcase, **omxplorer**, is a data app in the spirit of Numbers and Power BI, and the app itself is about 2,100 lines of Mojo, built from the framework's components.

## What it feels like

### The sentence is the interface

In omxplorer a chart's title isn't a label. It *is* the chart:

> **Sum** of **revenue** by **product**, **largest first**, **top 5**, **every row**, as **bars**

Every coloured word is a setting: tap it and pick another. Or type into the ask field: *"median"*, *"by month, as a line"*, *"only paid and over 5,000"*. The sentence rewrites itself, and the bars animate to the new answer. A person, a keyboard and an agent all edit the same sentence.

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/img/readme-sheet.jpg" alt="omxplorer's sheet: 1,000,000 orders, and a chart whose title is a sentence of tappable settings, 'Sum of revenue by product, largest first, top 5, every row, as bars', answered in 0.7 ms on the GPU" width="100%">
  <br><sub>1,000,000 rows. The chart answered "revenue by product, largest first, top 5" in 0.7 ms on an RTX 3090. The inspector on the right shows the same sentence as four pages: Data, Order, Rows, Style.</sub>
</p>

### It shows its work

Every answer says how long it took and where it ran ("0.7 ms on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090"). A tile says what it's made of ("p50 exact", "of 1,000,000 values"). And when you ask for something it can't do, it tells you what it skipped instead of quietly guessing. For example, "under 2.5" on a whole-number column, or a second number condition, is left out and named.

### It's quiet

The toolbar only inserts things; the inspector sets them up, and shows only the settings that apply. One accent colour per mode (green for the sheet, red for the report). Motion is short and springy: hover and press in 150 ms or less, tiles in 320 ms, and nothing overshoots.

## Agent native, from the first line

Most apps meet AI agents through the screen: screenshots, pixel coordinates, an accessibility tree written for screen readers, or an API someone added later. omxcode takes a different route. **The agent is a host**, the same way GTK and the browser are.

The view tree that GTK turns into widgets and the web turns into HTML, the agent host turns into **tools** ([docs/agent.md](docs/agent.md)):

- **No per-app work.** A button's tag names its tool, its tooltip describes it, and tapping it is calling it. A menu item becomes `file-save`. A text field becomes a tool that takes `text`. Every app built with omxcode is an MCP server already (29 components are proven through the agent so far; the matrix below has the rest).
- **An agent can do nothing a person couldn't.** A disabled button is no tool. A dialog's buttons are tools only while it is open. The screen is the permission model.
- **It gets back what changed, in words.** It doesn't have to compare two screenshots. Each call returns the new texts, what opened or closed, and the tools that appeared or went.
- **It reads, not just clicks.** `read` gives the screen's text grouped by area, or a grid's rows as tab-separated text. `render` gives a drawn view as a PNG for agents that can see.
- **The same sentence.** The chart sentence a person taps is the one the agent asks. There's no separate agent API to drift out of date.

This is a real session, run today against omxplorer and a 1M-row file. It uses no screenshots and no coordinates:

```text
→ choose-a-file  {"path": "orders_1m.csv"}
→ create-table
→ insert-chart
→ ask            {"text": "revenue by product, largest first, top 5", "submit": true}
← Did ask.
  Now: chart0: 0.6 ms
  Now: inspector: Sum of revenue by product, largest first, top 5, every row, as bars
  Now: status-bar: Took revenue · by product · largest first · top 5
→ read
← menubar: orders_1m · 1,000,000 rows
  menubar: ● NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 · ready
  status-bar: Rows 1,000,000 · Columns 12 · Sum 114,007,922.00 …
```

Give any omxcode app to Claude Code with one command:

```bash
scripts/agent.sh omxplorer     # prints: claude mcp add omxplorer -- pixi run python mojoui/hosts/agent.py build/omxplorer/web
```

The charts speak an agent's language too. They are [Flint](https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/) specs, the chart format Microsoft designed for AI agents. omxcode draws them natively, and the same specs run through Flint's own renderer as a cross-check.

> [!NOTE]
> **What the agent can't do yet:** read a chart's figures as text (it reads the sentence and can `render` the picture), read a drawn grid's cells in apps other than omxplorer, drag objects on a page, or generate new UI. Generated UI over AG-UI is next, built on the same operations log.

## Under the hood

The choices, and why each was made.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["<b>app.mojo</b><br/>view() · update()"]:::app
    A --> L["GTK 4"]:::host
    A --> W["Web · FastHTML"]:::host
    A --> D["Android views"]:::host
    A --> M["AppKit"]:::host
    A --> I["UIKit"]:::host
    A --> G["Agent · MCP tools"]:::agent
    A -. "same language" .-> K["GPU · MX frame"]:::gpu
    classDef app fill:#0b0b0d,stroke:#0b0b0d,color:#ffffff
    classDef host fill:#f6f8fb,stroke:#c9ced6,color:#1b1f24
    classDef agent fill:#f6f8fb,stroke:#0b0b0d,color:#0b0b0d
    classDef gpu fill:#f6f8fb,stroke:#c9ced6,color:#1b1f24
```

| Layer | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Language** | **Mojo** for the app, the UI framework and the GPU code | Reads like Python, compiles to native code, and runs the same functions on the GPU. One language from button to kernel. |
| **App model** | `view()` describes the screen from state; `update(event)` changes it | The model of Elm, SwiftUI and React. Hosts patch only what changed: after a sheet opens, an edit rebuilds **at most 15 widgets**. |
| **Native controls** | GTK 4 · HTML · Android views · AppKit · UIKit | The platform's own look, keyboard, text input and screen reader. Mojo calls C and Objective-C directly, with no binding generator. |
| **Drawn views** | A **Scene**: a display list in keyed layers, replayed as GPU render nodes (GTK today) | A 1M-row grid at 2180×1074 px scrolls at **0.8 ms p95 a frame**, against 14.2 ms for painted pixels: 18–75× cheaper, 0 texture uploads. |
| **Data engine** | **MX frame**, a Mojo dataframe engine on the GPU | Sum, median and p90 per group, number conditions, calendar groups. **100M rows** (a 4 GB table) stream from disk and **open in 0.2 s**. |
| **Web** | **FastHTML** server; HTMX patches the page | One app state per tab, shared GPU data per process, no app JavaScript. |
| **Agent** | A hand-written **MCP** server over the same module the web serves | The view tree becomes tools; see above. |
| **Charts** | **Flint** specs, drawn natively | One chart language for people, agents and every host. |
| **Looks** | Themes as plugins (`themes/`): Liquid, Ledger, Graphite, Blueprint, Fluent, Omarchy, Paper | The framework names no theme (a check proves it). With no theme, an app looks like its platform. |
| **Proof** | `scripts/check`: every goal, re-run on GTK, in Chromium and on the Android emulator | Results compared with pyarrow, pixels diffed, real input used. A goal isn't done until the reviewer passes it. |

### Measured

<p>
  <img alt="1M-row chart 0.6 ms" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/1M--row%20chart-0.6%20ms-1d1d21?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=0b0b0d">
  <img alt="grid scroll 0.8 ms a frame" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/grid%20scroll-0.8%20ms%20a%20frame-1d1d21?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=0b0b0d">
  <img alt="20M points 1.5 ms" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/20M%20points-1.5%20ms-1d1d21?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=0b0b0d">
  <img alt="100M rows open in 0.2 s" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/100M%20rows-open%20in%200.2%20s-1d1d21?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=0b0b0d">
</p>

All on one Linux machine with an RTX 3090, and all from the checks or their benchmarks.

**Benchmarks:** omxcode against plain JS, JS + WebGPU and Rust (wasm and native) on one particle field, every table, caveat and line of code: [docs/benchmarks.md](docs/benchmarks.md).

| What | Time |
|---|---|
| A chart over 1M rows (sum by group) | **0.5–0.7 ms** |
| A median per group over 1M rows | **6.4 ms** |
| The status bar's sum and average over 1M rows | **0.3 ms** |
| Scrolling the 1M-row grid, per frame (p95) | **0.8 ms** |
| The Data Lens: 20M points counted and coloured, one 1080p frame | **1.5 ms** (130 ms on the CPU, same pixels) |
| A Power BI-style dashboard re-aggregating 20M rows per click | **6–9 ms** |
| Opening a 100M-row file, streamed | **0.2 s** |

> [!NOTE]
> **The honest edge:** at 100M rows in memory a median chart takes about 0.7 s, and today the window waits for it. Moving that work off the UI thread is next.

## Where it stands

**Runs** means a script runs it on that platform. **Builds** means it builds but no check runs it there yet. The full matrix is generated from the code: [docs/components.md](docs/components.md).

| Host | Runs | Builds | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Linux** (GTK 4) | 78 | 1 | Every component, gesture and theme; omxplorer's home |
| **Web** (FastHTML) | 79 | 0 | The same results as Linux, checked in Chromium |
| **Agent** (MCP) | 29 | 17 | Every app, no per-app work |
| **Android** (views over JNI) | 19 | 16 | runs the classic controls on the emulator; the newer ones are still to come |
| **Mac** (AppKit) | 0 | 60 | Builds and signs; not proven by a check yet |
| **iPhone** (UIKit) | 0 | 61 | Builds and signs; not proven by a check yet |

The GPU path is NVIDIA today. Apple and phone GPUs use the CPU path, which runs the same functions.

**Why Mojo, honestly.** Mojo is young (1.1). It has a small ecosystem, no official iPhone, Android or WebAssembly target (omxcode cross-compiles with two hand-written runtime functions), and no Windows release yet. Flutter, React Native and the Rust kits are far ahead on maturity, tooling and production users. What none of them has is one readable language from the button to the GPU kernel, with native controls on every platform and an agent built in as a host.

## Try it

You need x86-64 Linux with GTK 4 and libadwaita 1.7+, [pixi](https://pixi.sh), and an NVIDIA GPU for the GPU path (without one, the CPU path runs the same code).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/abhisheksreesaila/omxcode && cd omxcode
pixi install                                   # Mojo 1.1, MAX, FastHTML
scripts/omxplorer.sh                           # omxplorer, native window
scripts/omxplorer.sh web                       # the same app at http://127.0.0.1:5001
scripts/check                                  # rebuild everything and re-prove every goal
```

> [!NOTE]
> If `pixi install` stops at `failed to link 'share/X11/xkb'`, two conda-forge packages (Xvfb and xkeyboard-config) raced for one path. Remove the half-made env and run it again: `rm -rf .pixi && pixi install`.

> [!TIP]
> Insert → Chart, then type into its ask field: *median*, *by month, as a line*, or *only paid and over 5,000*. Or tap any coloured word in the chart's title.

The smallest app is one file (trimmed from `examples/hello/app.mojo`):

```mojo
struct Main(App):
    var clicks: Int

    def update(mut self, event: Event):
        if event.message == GREET:
            self.clicks += 1

    def view(self) -> View:
        return VStack(
            Text("Hello, Ada! (" + String(self.clicks) + ")", style=TITLE),
            Button("Greet", on_tap=GREET, style=PROMINENT),
        )
```

`scripts/build.sh hello all` turns it into a GTK app, a web app, a Mac app and an iPhone app; `scripts/build.sh hello android` makes the APK.

# mojo-ui reference

The API in one page: the app model, every component, layout, the GPU canvas, the examples. The story is in the [README](../README.md); how the pieces fit is in [architecture.md](architecture.md); the agent host in [agent.md](agent.md).

## The app model

Here is a complete app in one file: no project setup, no platform folders.

```mojo
from mojoui import App, Event, View, VStack, Text, Button, TITLE, PROMINENT

comptime GREET = 1                         # a message: "the Greet button was tapped"


struct Main(App):
    var clicks: Int                        # the app's state

    def __init__(out self):
        self.clicks = 0

    def title(self) -> String:
        return "Hello"

    def update(mut self, event: Event):    # state changes only here
        if event.message == GREET:
            self.clicks += 1

    def view(self) -> View:                # the screen, described from the state
        return VStack(
            Text("Hello, Ada! (" + String(self.clicks) + ")", style=TITLE),
            Button("Greet", on_tap=GREET, style=PROMINENT),
        )
```

```bash
scripts/build.sh hello all          # → Linux app, web module, Mac app, iPhone app
scripts/build.sh hello android      # → Android app (.apk)
```

That's the whole model, the same one as Elm, SwiftUI and React: **state → `view()` → screen**, and **tap → `update()` → new state**. You never touch GTK, HTML, AppKit or UIKit; `scripts/check` enforces it. (This is a trimmed `examples/hello/app.mojo`.)

On Linux the Greet button is a GTK button and on the web an HTML `<button>`; the Mac and iPhone builds make an `NSButton` and a `UIButton` (Liquid Glass on iOS 26), though those haven't run on real hardware yet. Native widgets bring their platform's own look, keyboard handling, text input and screen-reader support, instead of an imitation.

## Components

| Component | Does | Linux | Web | Mac | iPhone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Text(text, style=TITLE\|HEADLINE\|BODY\|CAPTION)` | a label | GtkLabel | h1/h3/p | NSTextField label | UILabel (Dynamic Type) |
| `Button(title, on_tap=, style=PLAIN\|PROMINENT\|DESTRUCTIVE)` | sends a message | GtkButton | button | NSButton | UIButton (glass) |
| `TextField(value, placeholder=, on_change=, on_submit=)` | one line of text; `event.text` | GtkEntry | input | NSTextField | UITextField |
| `Toggle(label, on, on_toggle=)` | on/off; `event.number` 1/0 | GtkCheckButton | checkbox | checkbox | UISwitch |
| `Dropdown(options, selected, on_select=)` | pick one; `event.number`, `event.text` | GtkDropDown | select | NSPopUpButton | menu button |
| `Slider(value, on_change=)` | 0–100 | GtkScale | range | NSSlider | UISlider |
| `ProgressBar(value)` | 0–100 | GtkProgressBar | progress | NSProgressIndicator | UIProgressView |
| `Image(pixels, width, height)` | RGBA pixels | GtkPicture | PNG img | NSImageView | UIImageView |
| `Segmented(options, selected, on_select=)` | a few joined choices | AdwToggleGroup | radio buttons styled as a segmented control | NSSegmentedControl | UISegmentedControl |
| `Radio(options, selected, on_select=)` | pick one from a list | GtkCheckButton group | radio inputs | NSButton radios | buttons with circle symbols |
| `TextArea(value, placeholder=, on_change=, height=)` | several lines of text | GtkTextView | textarea | NSTextView | UITextView |
| `Alert(title, message, buttons, on_choose=)` | a modal question, shown while it's in the view; `event.number` = button | AdwAlertDialog | dialog | NSAlert | UIAlertController |
| `Tabs(sections, selected, on_select=)` | switch sections | AdwToggleGroup | tabs (radio inputs) | NSSegmentedControl | UISegmentedControl |
| `NavBar(title, on_back=)` | a screen's title bar, with Back | header box + back button | header | back button + title | UINavigationBar |
| `DatePicker("YYYY-MM-DD", on_change=)` | pick a date | GtkCalendar | input type=date | NSDatePicker | UIDatePicker (compact) |
| `Icon(name, size=)` | one of the shared icons (`ICON_NAMES`) | Adwaita symbolic icons | Lucide SVG (vendored) | SF Symbols | SF Symbols |
| `Grid(items, columns)` | items in rows of N | GtkGrid | CSS grid | rows of NSStackView | rows of UIStackView |
| `LazyList(count, list_id, on_tap=)` | a long list; only rows on screen are built, from `App.row(list_id, index)` | GtkListView | windowed rows fetched while scrolling | NSTableView data source | UITableView data source |
| `VStack(...)`, `HStack(...)` | layout; also from a `List[View]` for rows | GtkBox | flexbox | NSStackView | UIStackView |
| `Scroll(view, height=)` | scrolls tall content | GtkScrolledWindow | overflow | NSScrollView | UIScrollView |
| `Divider()`, `Spacer()` | a line; empty space | | | | |

See them in `examples/gallery/app.mojo` and `examples/kitchen/app.mojo`.


## Layout

Chain layout settings onto any view. They use flexbox names, and each platform's **own** layout system does the work: GtkBox (plus CSS padding) on Linux, CSS flexbox on the web, and NSStackView/UIStackView with Auto Layout on Apple. There's no layout engine in between, just a thin translation.

```mojo
HStack(
    Text("Total").grow(),                   # takes the free space in the row
    Text(money(total)),
    Button("Pay", on_tap=PAY).width(120),   # fixed width
).justify(BETWEEN).padding(12, 16).fill()   # spread out, padded, full width of its column
```

| Setting | Meaning | Flexbox equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `.padding(all)`, `.padding(vertical, horizontal)` | space inside the view's edges | `padding` |
| `.width(n)`, `.height(n)` | fixed size, including padding | `width`, `height` (border-box) |
| `.min_width(n)`, `.max_width(n)` | size limits; text wraps within a max width | `min-width`, `max-width` |
| `.grow()` | take the free space along the parent stack | `flex: 1` |
| `.fill()` | stretch across the parent stack | `align-self: stretch` |
| `.align(START\|CENTER\|END\|STRETCH)` | on a stack: line children up across it | `align-items` |
| `.justify(START\|CENTER\|END\|BETWEEN)` | on a stack: place children along it | `justify-content` |
| `.tag(name)` | name a view, for tests and accessibility | `data-tag` |

Stacks centre their children unless you say otherwise. Every setting is proven by measuring the real widgets on GTK and in Chromium (`examples/layout/app.mojo`, checked by `scripts/check`). Layout isn't pixel-identical across platforms, because fonts and control sizes differ, but the relations are the same: offsets, fixed sizes, who takes the free space.

## Canvas: draw it yourself (on the GPU when there is one)

Native controls can't show 20 million data points. A `Canvas` is a surface the app paints itself, sized by the layout like any other view; everything around it stays native. Each platform maps it onto its own image surface, display clock and gesture system: a GtkPicture with GTK's frame clock and drag/scroll/zoom gestures; a `<canvas>` on the web; an NSImageView or UIImageView with a CADisplayLink and pan/pinch recognisers on Apple.

```mojo
def view(self) -> View:
    return HStack(
        sidebar,                                                    # native controls
        Canvas(0, self.version, on_gesture=GESTURE, on_frame=FRAME if self.playing else NO_MSG).grow().fill(),
    )

def draw(mut self, canvas: Int, mut surface: Surface):             # hosts call this at the canvas's real pixel size
    var hits = self.cloud.bin[place](surface.width, surface.height, self.knobs())
    self.cloud.shade[colour](surface, self.knobs())

def update(mut self, event: Event):
    if event.message == GESTURE and event.number == PAN:
        self.centre_x -= event.dx * self.units_per_point()         # event.dx, dy: points moved
        self.version += 1                                           # a new version → hosts redraw
```

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Canvas(id, version, on_gesture=, on_frame=)` | a view the app paints; hosts call `draw(id, surface)` again when `version` changes or the canvas is resized |
| `def draw(mut self, canvas: Int, mut surface: Surface)` | an `App` method (default: blank). It may also update state shown elsewhere (e.g. how long drawing took); hosts refresh the rest of the screen afterwards |
| `Surface` | RGBA pixels: `width`, `height` (pixels), `scale` (pixels per point), `set(x, y, rgba(...))`, `get`, `fill`, `points_width()` |
| `on_gesture` | `event.number` is `PAN` (`event.dx`, `dy` in points), `ZOOM` (`event.zoom`, a factor, around `event.x`, `y`) or `TAP` (`event.x`, `y`). Drags, wheels (4 notches = 2×), trackpad and touch pinches |
| `on_frame` | one event per display frame while set (`event.number` = microseconds since the last); set it to `NO_MSG` to stop |
| `def window_size(self)` | the window's starting size on desktops (default 480 × 560) |

**`mojoui.gpu`** runs plain Mojo functions over millions of points: `PointCloud(x, y, a, b)` takes four float32 columns (what a dataframe hands over) and keeps them on the GPU. `cloud.bin[place](w, h, knobs)` calls `place(point, w, h, knobs) -> pixel index` (or `OUTSIDE`/`FILTERED`) once per point and counts hits per pixel; `cloud.shade[colour](surface, knobs)` turns each count into a colour. With a GPU on Linux (NVIDIA tested; AMD is supported by MAX but untested here) both run as GPU kernels and the data stays on the GPU between frames; without one, the very same functions run on the CPU (Mac and iPhone builds use the CPU for now).

**Web:** the Mojo app runs in the server. The page pulls one JPEG frame at a time from it, at most once per display refresh, and sends gestures back as ordinary events. The JavaScript is a small fixed adapter in `mojoui/hosts/web.py`; apps never contain any.

## Examples
- `examples/analytics/app.mojo`: **Contoso Retail**, the analytics showcase (above).
- `examples/lens/app.mojo`: **Data Lens**, the GPU showcase. 20 million trips in a made-up city, drawn live as a density map: pick a kind (taxi, rideshare, bike), slide through the hours or press Play to watch a day go by, drag, scroll or pinch to explore. Every frame re-counts all 20 million trips: **1.5–1.6 ms per 1080p frame on an RTX 3090** (130–140 ms on the CPU, same pixels; across runs). 59 fps on GTK on a 60 Hz display; streamed to the browser at 60 fps (measured in headless Chromium on the same machine, after 10 warm-up frames; a real network adds latency and bandwidth). Built for desktop: on a phone the 340-point sidebar leaves little room for the map (a phone layout is still to do).
- `examples/hello/app.mojo`: the smallest app.
- `examples/gallery/app.mojo`: every component, wired to some state.
- `examples/kitchen/app.mojo`: every component added in goal 4 (tabs, a details screen, alert, date, icons, grid, a 10,000-row list).
- `examples/expenses/app.mojo`: **Pocket Expenses**, a small real app using all of them:
  - add an expense (amount, category, date, note);
  - browse 5,000 of them in a list that only draws what's on screen;
  - open one, and confirm deleting it;
  - see totals by category in a grid with icons.
- `examples/todo/app.mojo`: a real todo: type and press Return or Add, tick tasks done, filter All/Active/Done, remove, clear done.
- `examples/gpu/app.mojo`: a **GPU** fractal. A plain Mojo function, `mandelbrot(x, y, …)`, runs once per pixel on the NVIDIA GPU via `mojoui/gpu.mojo`: 480×320 pixels in about 0.1 ms, against about 40–80 ms on the CPU, and checked to match the CPU pixel for pixel. Linux and web (it needs an NVIDIA GPU; AMD untested).

## Write your own app
1. Make a folder in `examples/` with an `app.mojo` that defines `struct Main(App)`: `__init__`, `title()`, `update(event)`, `view()`.
2. Messages are `Int` constants (`comptime ADD = 1`); `event.text` and `event.number` carry values.
3. Build with `scripts/build.sh` and the folder name, e.g. `scripts/build.sh hello all`. An optional `platforms` file in the folder limits which platforms `all` means.

The app file imports only `mojoui`; it never touches GTK, HTML, AppKit or UIKit (`scripts/check` enforces this).

How the pieces fit together, platform by platform: [architecture.md](architecture.md).

## More showcases

### Analytics on the GPU

`examples/analytics/app.mojo` is a Power BI-style dashboard in one Mojo file: **20 million order lines re-aggregated every time you click**, with KPIs, revenue by month, category and region, order sizes and top products. Tap a bar, a column or a month and every other chart filters (crossfiltering).

- **Every chart is a [Flint](https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/) spec**, the chart language Microsoft built for AI agents. mojoui draws Flint specs natively (the same pixels on every platform), and the same specs run through Flint's own Vega-Lite backend: all nine are checked that way.
- **Three engines behind one switch:** Mojo GPU kernels (**6–9 ms** for all seven aggregations over 20M rows, depending on the filters), the same functions on one CPU core (about 750 ms), and **MX frame**, a Mojo dataframe engine (about 115 ms on the CPU). A test compares every one of the seven results across all three engines: they agree to the cent.
- **Controls in Fluent 2** on Linux and the web, from one design setting (`design() -> FLUENT`).

```bash
scripts/build.sh analytics linux && build/analytics/linux/analytics           # native window (Linux)
scripts/build.sh analytics web && pixi run python mojoui/hosts/web.py build/analytics/web   # → http://127.0.0.1:5001
```

Linux and the web for now. The Mac version is waiting on a Python-free MX frame API (`docs/mxframe-mojo-api.md`). On the web the 20M rows are built once per server process and shared by every tab (`App.init_shared()`), so many viewers can sit on one GPU.

### The Workbook

`examples/workbook/app.mojo` is a Numbers-style page over the same engine: **tables, pivots, charts and notes side by side, sharing one set of 20 million rows**. Columns, never cell addresses.

![The Workbook on Linux: a table, a pivot, two charts and a note on one page](gallery/img/workbook-linux.png)

- **Edit a cell, add a row, delete a row, sort, undo.** Edits never copy the data: a session keeps a sparse overlay, the GPU aggregates the shared rows, and the overlay's deltas are applied exactly (`mojoui/frame.mojo`, `frame_gpu.mojo`).
- **Formula columns** typed as text (`margin = cents - cost`, `bin = min(cents // 50, 23)`): a column-level dependency graph, evaluated inside the GPU group-by kernel, so they cost no memory.
- **Pivots** are run-time group-bys on the GPU (rows × columns × value, about a millisecond for 20M rows); **charts** are Flint specs; tap a bar and everything else filters.
- **Drag objects** by their header, resize by the corner, snap to an 8-point grid (`Board`, a new container); narrow windows and phones show the objects as a list.
- **Save/Open** a workbook folder: `workbook.json` (objects, formulas, your edits) plus Parquet for tables without a reproducible source. An agent can write it.
- **One copy per process:** `App.init_shared()` builds the rows and the GPU buffers once; every window or browser tab shares them.

```bash
scripts/workbook.sh          # the native Linux window
scripts/workbook.sh web      # → http://127.0.0.1:5001, every tab sharing the one GPU copy
```
The two-minute walkthrough is in [`docs/morning.md`](morning.md).

### The hybrid: native controls plus a GPU canvas

Native controls can't show 20 million points, so mojo-ui has one more view, `Canvas`. The app paints it itself, and everything around it stays native (trimmed from `examples/lens/app.mojo`):

```mojo
def view(self) -> View:
    return HStack(
        sidebar,                                           # native controls
        Canvas(0, self.version, on_gesture=GESTURE).grow().fill(),
    )

def draw(mut self, canvas: Int, mut surface: Surface):     # called at the canvas's real pixel size
    var k = self.knobs(self.units_per_point() / surface.scale)
    self.cloud.bin[place](surface.width, surface.height, k)   # runs on the GPU
    self.cloud.shade[colour](surface, k)
```

`place` and `colour` are ordinary Mojo functions. On a machine with a GPU they run as GPU kernels; without one, the very same functions run on the CPU. The **Data Lens** example (`examples/lens/app.mojo`) uses this to redraw 20 million trips:

| | Measured (RTX 3090) |
|---|---|
| One 1920×1080 frame, all 20M points counted and coloured | **1.5–1.6 ms** on the GPU (130–140 ms on the CPU, identical pixels) |
| Linux window, playing through the day | **59 fps** on a 60 Hz display |
| Browser (the server's GPU paints, frames are streamed) | **60 fps** in headless Chromium on the same machine |

![The same app in the browser](img/lens-web.png)

This is how many serious apps are built anyway: map and photo apps put native controls around a GPU surface, and Figma puts HTML around a WebGL canvas. The difference is that here both halves are one language and one file.

<!-- source: docs/architecture.md -->

# How mojo-ui works

This is the deep dive behind the [README](../README.md): what each layer does, how Mojo reaches each platform, and why it's built this way. Every choice links to its entry in [decisions.md](decisions.md) (D-nn).

## The big picture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph app["Your app (one Mojo file)"]
        S["state (a struct)"]
        U["update(event)"]
        V["view() → View"]
        D["draw(canvas, surface)"]
    end
    subgraph core["mojoui core (Mojo, platform-free)"]
        VT["view.mojo<br/>flat node list"]
        DF["diff.mojo<br/>patches or rebuild"]
        RT["app.mojo<br/>App trait, Event, Runtime"]
        GPU["gpu.mojo<br/>PointCloud, per-pixel kernels"]
    end
    subgraph hosts["Hosts (one per platform, also Mojo)"]
        GTK["gtk.mojo"]
        WEB["web.mojo + web.py"]
        AK["appkit.mojo"]
        UK["uikit.mojo"]
        AN["android.mojo"]
    end
    app --> core
    core --> hosts
    GTK --> L["GTK 4 / libadwaita<br/>(C)"]
    WEB --> P["FastHTML (Python)<br/>→ browser: HTML + HTMX"]
    AK --> AP["AppKit<br/>(Objective-C runtime)"]
    UK --> IP["UIKit<br/>(Objective-C runtime)"]
    AN --> JN["Android views<br/>(JNI)"]
    GPU --> MAX["MAX → NVIDIA GPU<br/>(AMD supported by MAX, untested)"]
```

Three layers, and only the bottom one knows any platform:

1. **Your app** describes the screen as data and changes its state in `update()`. It imports only `mojoui` (`scripts/check` rejects anything else).
2. **The core** turns "the screen before" and "the screen after" into a short list of changes. It's plain Mojo with no platform code, so it's unit-tested on its own (`tests/test_mojoui.mojo`, `tests/test_canvas.mojo`).
3. **A host per platform** creates real native widgets for the screen, wires their events back to the app, and applies the changes. Hosts are also Mojo.

## The core: screens are data

A `View` is a **flat list of nodes**; node 0 is the root and containers list their children by index (D-14). It's flat partly because Mojo 1.1 can't put a `List[View]` inside `View`, but flat lists are also easy to compare and to pair one-to-one with native widgets.

```mojo
VStack(Text("Hi"), Button("Go", on_tap=GO))
# → [VSTACK children=[1,2]] [TEXT "Hi"] [BUTTON "Go" msg=GO]
```

Every interaction follows the same loop, on every platform:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Widget as Native widget
    participant Host
    participant Runtime
    participant App
    User->>Widget: tap
    Widget->>Host: signal / action (C callback into Mojo)
    Host->>Runtime: dispatch(Event(message, text, number))
    Runtime->>App: update(event)
    Runtime->>App: view()
    Runtime->>Runtime: diff(old screen, new screen)
    Runtime-->>Host: patches (set text, set value…) or "rebuild"
    Host->>Widget: change only what changed
```

- **Messages are numbers** (`comptime GREET = 1`). A widget never holds a closure; the host looks up the message in the current screen when the event arrives (D-19), so a message can change without rewiring anything.
- **Patches or rebuild:** same shape means small patches (new label text, new slider value). A different shape (a row added) means the host rebuilds the window's content. Rebuilds wait for the next idle moment, never inside the widget's own event, because GTK and AppKit would otherwise destroy a widget while it's still handling a click.
- **Layout** uses flexbox names (`.padding()`, `.grow()`, `.fill()`, `.align()`, `.justify()`), and each host maps them onto the platform's own layout system: GtkBox, CSS flexbox, NSStackView/UIStackView with Auto Layout. There's no layout engine of our own (ROADMAP decision 10): the translation stays thin.

## The bridge: Mojo speaks C

Everything below the core rests on one fact: **Mojo can call C functions, and C can call Mojo functions**, with no binding generator in between.

- **Calling out:** `external_call["gtk_button_new_with_label", Int](title)` calls a C function directly. When one C function is needed with several signatures (GTK's `g_signal_connect_data`, Objective-C's `objc_msgSend`), the host looks the function up once with `dlsym` and casts its address to the exact signature of each call (`ccall`, `msg`; D-02, D-10).
- **Calling in:** a Mojo function marked `abi("C")` is an ordinary C function pointer. GTK signal handlers, Objective-C methods and GPU kernels are all plain Mojo functions passed by address.
- **The platform owns the loop** (ROADMAP decision 2): GTK's main loop, `NSApplication run`, `UIApplicationMain` and the web server call into Mojo, never the other way round. iPhone requires this, and it works the same everywhere.

On Linux, Mac and iPhone there's no JSON and no message bus between the app and the screen: the app's state and the widgets live in one process and one memory. (The web host passes the screen to Python as JSON, inside one process.)

## Linux: GTK through C

`mojoui/hosts/gtk.mojo` builds GTK 4 widgets (with libadwaita's styling) for each node: `GtkLabel`, `GtkButton`, `GtkEntry`, `GtkDropDown`, `AdwToggleGroup`, `GtkListView`, `AdwAlertDialog` and so on.

- **Events** are GTK signals connected to Mojo functions. The handler finds its node from data stored on the widget and calls `send()`.
- **Re-entrancy:** GTK fires signals *while* we change widgets (setting a slider's value fires "value-changed"). A busy flag stops those echoes. It's kept on the GApplication object rather than in a Mojo field, because the compiler may assume a Mojo field can't change during a `mut self` method (journal, goal 3).
- **Canvas:** a `GtkPicture` showing a texture made from the app's pixels; a GTK tick callback (GTK's display clock) sends frame events and redraws; GTK's own drag, scroll, zoom and click gestures become PAN/ZOOM/TAP events. Ticks stop when nothing needs drawing, so an idle app doesn't wake the CPU (D-64).
- **Testing:** with `MOJOUI_TEST="tap:Greet;type:Name=Ada"` the same binary drives its real widgets through their normal APIs, prints what GTK reports, and quits. `scripts/check` uses this.

## Mac and iPhone: the Objective-C runtime, from Mojo

There is no Swift and no C in the Apple apps (D-01, ROADMAP decision 9). AppKit and UIKit are Objective-C frameworks, and Objective-C is a thin layer over a C runtime, so Mojo can talk to it directly:

- **Every call is a message:** `msg(button, "setTitle:", ns_string("Go"))` is `objc_msgSend(button, sel("setTitle:"), …)`, cast to that call's C signature (`mojoui/hosts/objc.mojo`).
- **Our own classes, made at run time:** `MojoTarget` (receives every control's action), `MojoCanvas` (an image view whose `scrollWheel:` is Mojo), and the iPhone's app and scene delegates are created with `objc_allocateClassPair`. Their methods are Mojo `abi("C")` functions.
- **Finding the node:** each control's `tag` packs the host's address and the node index (D-18).
- **Structs by value:** on Apple Silicon a CGRect or CGPoint travels in floating-point registers, the same as four (or two) separate doubles. Mojo passes and receives them that way, checked in the compiled code (D-03, journal goal 6).
- **Built on Linux:** Mojo cross-compiles to arm64 macOS/iOS object files; `ld64.lld` links them against small text stubs that only name Apple's libraries (D-05); the few Mojo runtime functions an app needs are themselves written in Mojo (`mojoui/hosts/mojo_rt.mojo`, D-04); `rcodesign` signs (D-09).
- **Canvas:** an NSImageView/UIImageView showing a CGImage of the app's pixels, a CADisplayLink for frames, and the platform's pan, pinch and tap recognisers.

**Not yet run on real hardware.** The calls are reviewed, the binaries are checked (entry point, linked libraries, only Apple system functions, signature), but nobody has launched them on a Mac or iPhone yet.

## The web: Mojo inside a Python web server

Mojo can't compile to WebAssembly yet (probed in goal 6), so the web version runs the Mojo app **on the server** and sends the browser plain HTML:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph server["Server process"]
        M["your app.mojo<br/>compiled as a Python module<br/>(mojoui_app.so)"]
        F["FastHTML (Python)<br/>mojoui/hosts/web.py"]
        G["GPU (MAX)"]
        F <-->|"view JSON, events, patches"| M
        M --> G
    end
    subgraph browser["Browser"]
        H["plain HTML controls<br/>(the browser's own widgets)"]
        X["HTMX<br/>(vendored, pinned)"]
        C["canvas adapter<br/>(small fixed JS)"]
    end
    F -->|"HTML, out-of-band swaps"| H
    X -->|"POST /e (an event)"| F
    C -->|"GET /frame (pull one JPEG)"| F
    C -->|"gestures as events"| F
```

- **Mojo as a Python module:** `hosts/web_main.mojo` builds the app as a Python extension (`PythonModuleBuilder`). FastHTML keeps one app session per browser tab and calls `event()`, `view()` and `draw()` on it.
- **HTML and HTMX:** each node becomes a standard HTML control (`<button>`, `<input>`, `<select>`), so the browser draws its own native widgets. HTMX posts each event to the server; the server answers with just the changed controls as out-of-band swaps. Apart from the canvas adapter there is no custom JavaScript.
- **Canvas on the web:** a small fixed adapter in `web.py` pulls one JPEG frame at a time, painted by the Mojo app (on the server's GPU) at the canvas's real pixel size. It pulls at most once per display refresh, and a new pull starts only when the last frame has arrived, so a slow network gets fewer frames instead of a backlog (D-57, D-58). Gestures go back through HTMX as ordinary events.
- **Python's ecosystem, for free:** the app runs inside Python, so the server side can use any Python library, and the web host is FastHTML, a stack this project's owner already uses.
- **JavaScript's ecosystem, planned:** "islands" (ROADMAP decision 7) will let a node mount a JS library (a chart, a map, a code editor) into a placeholder, with a 10–30 line adapter per library, sending only meaningful events back to Mojo.

**Why the server, for now:** it works today, the browser stays tiny, and the server's GPU and Python libraries are right there. The costs are a round trip per interaction, bandwidth for canvas frames, and memory per tab (the Data Lens builds its 20M-point dataset per tab, D-60). When Mojo gains a WebAssembly target, the same app file can run in the browser instead.

## Android: JNI, from Mojo

Android's views are Java objects, and JNI (Java's C interface) gives native code a table of functions to create and call them. `mojoui/hosts/jni.mojo` calls those functions by their slot in the table, cast to each call's C signature: the same role `objc_msgSend` plays on Apple (D-67). `mojoui/hosts/android.mojo` maps the view tree onto `LinearLayout`, `TextView`, `Button`, `EditText`, `Switch`, `Spinner`, `SeekBar`, `RadioGroup`, `ListView` and `ImageView`, with layout settings as `LayoutParams`, weights and gravity.

- **The one Java file:** Android only calls a *Java object* back (a click listener, a text watcher, a list adapter, a frame callback). `mojoui/hosts/android/MojoActivity.java` (78 lines, framework only) is the Activity: it loads the Mojo library and forwards every callback to it (D-66).
- **Canvas:** an `ImageView` showing a bitmap of the app's pixels, `Choreographer` for frames, touch events turned into PAN/ZOOM/TAP. Android builds use the CPU path.
- **Proven on the emulator** with real input from `adb` (`scripts/android_drive.py`): the same steps as GTK and the web end in the same state. Not yet on a physical phone. Details: `docs/android.md`.

## The GPU

`mojoui/gpu.mojo` uses MAX (Modular's GPU runtime). The app writes **ordinary Mojo functions** and passes them as compile-time parameters; Mojo compiles them into GPU kernels:

- **Per-pixel:** `gpu.render[shade](w, h, params)` runs `shade(x, y, …) -> colour` once per pixel (the fractal example).
- **Point clouds:** `PointCloud(x, y, a, b)` uploads four float32 columns once. Each frame, `bin[place]` runs `place(point) -> pixel` for every point and counts the hits per pixel with atomic adds; `shade[colour]` turns each count into a colour; one copy brings the pixels back. That's 1.5–1.6 ms for 20 million points at 1080p on an RTX 3090 (across runs).
- **Same functions on the CPU:** without a GPU, `bin` and `shade` call the same `place` and `colour` on the CPU, so results are identical, just slower (checked pixel for pixel).
- **Apple:** the GPU path is compiled out of Mac and iPhone builds (`comptime if CompilationTarget.is_linux()`, D-56). MAX's Apple GPU runtime can't go into these runtime-free builds yet, so they use the CPU path.

## Why this design, for now

| Option | Good | Why not (for now) |
|---|---|---|
| **Our own GPU renderer for everything** (Flutter-style) | pixel-identical everywhere | rebuilds text input, accessibility and the platform's feel; a project of its own |
| **A web view everywhere** (Electron/Tauri-style) | the whole web stack | a browser in a box; GPU and data work in a second language |
| **Native skins in Swift/Kotlin fed with JSON** (ROADMAP decision 4, superseded by 9) | familiar tools on each platform | several codebases again, and data copied between languages |
| **Native widgets driven straight from Mojo, plus GPU canvases** (chosen) | native look and behaviour, one language, one memory, the GPU in the same file | each platform needs a host (once, in the framework); the web runs on the server until Mojo targets WebAssembly |

The deciding reason is the owner's vision: **one language, a very thin layer between the code you write and what runs**, with no app code in any other language.

## How it's proven

- `scripts/check` rebuilds everything from scratch and proves each milestone of the current goal (`GOAL.md`), plus every earlier goal's checks. It drives the real GTK widgets and a real headless Chromium with the same steps (`scripts/drive.py`), and requires both to end in identical states.
- Unit tests for the core (`tests/`), a GPU vs CPU benchmark (`tests/bench_lens.mojo`), and checks on the Apple binaries (allowed symbols, linked libraries, entry point, signature).
- Every goal ends with a reviewer pass; reports, decisions and dead ends are in `docs/`.


---

<!-- source: docs/agent.md -->

# The agent host: an omxcode app as MCP tools

The agent is a fifth host (D-160). GTK, the web, the iPad and the Mac each turn an app's tree of views into their own
widgets; `mojoui/hosts/agent.py` turns it into tools for an agent, over MCP on stdio, from the same `mojoui_app` module
the web host serves. An app changes nothing to be driven by an agent: the tag names the tool, the tooltip describes it,
the message is the call. **An agent can do nothing a person couldn't:** a disabled item is no tool, a dialog's or a
context menu's items are tools only while it is open.

## Give an app to Claude Code
```
scripts/agent.sh omxplorer          # builds build/omxplorer/web if needed, prints the one command:
claude mcp add omxplorer -- pixi run python …/mojoui/hosts/agent.py …/build/omxplorer/web
```
Any MCP client works the same way (the server speaks JSON-RPC over stdio, one object per line; D-161). By hand:
```
pixi run python scripts/agent_client.py build/kit/web screen
pixi run python scripts/agent_client.py build/kit/web open-dialog
pixi run python scripts/agent_client.py build/omxplorer/web read name=grid count=5
```

## The tools
Four are always there:
- **screen** · what the app shows right now, as text: every view, the menus with their items and shortcuts, the open
  dialog, toast or popover, and the list of tools a person could use on it.
- **act** · one tool by name, with its value (`{"name": "settings-ledger-graphite-blueprint", "value": {"option": "Graphite"}}`).
  The same as calling the tool directly.
- **read** · the texts on screen (grouped by their tagged container, e.g. `status-bar: Sum 114,007,922.00`); with a
  name, one view's content: a drawn view's rows as tab-separated text where the app offers them (`App.describe`,
  D-163: omxplorer's grid), or a list's rows.
- **render** · a drawn view as a PNG (`{"name": "grid", "width": 900, "height": 400}`), for an agent that can see.

The rest come from the screen (D-162):
| On screen | Tool | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A menu item | `file-save`, `view-skin-graphite` (menu › submenu › item) | — |
| A button with a tag | its tag: `popover-button` | — |
| A button without one | a slug of its title: `open-dialog` | — |
| A file picker | its title: `open-file` | `path` |
| A text field | its tag or placeholder | `text`, `submit` |
| A checkbox or switch | its label: `show-grid-lines` | `on` |
| Segmented, radio, dropdown, tabs | its tag or its options: `ledger-graphite-blueprint` | `option` |
| A slider, a list | its tag | `value`, `row` |
| A canvas | its tag: `canvas`, `grid` | `gesture` (tap, double, secondary, press, release, key, pan, zoom), `x`, `y`, `key`, `modifiers` |
| A context menu's items | the item: `sort-z-a`; `close-menu` | — |
| A dialog's or popover's content | its title first: `settings-done`, `settings-show-grid-lines`; `close-dialog`, `close-popover` | as above |
| A toast | its action: `undo`; `dismiss-toast` | — |

After every call the server sends `notifications/tools/list_changed` (D-164): call `screen` or `tools/list` again to
see what the screen offers now. A wrong name or value comes back as an error result that lists the tools, so the agent
can correct itself.

## JavaScript widgets, and attaching to a running host (goal 34b)
A `WebComponent` is a tool pair, named by its tag (or, without one, its custom element's tag):
- **`<name>-read`** · what the widget describes: its `describe(el)` result as JSON (`{text, value, …}`). The editor:
  `mx-editor#1: {"text": "42 characters, cursor at 42: …", "value": "Agents can write here\nand on a second line", "lines": 2, …}`.
  A widget without `describe` reads `mx-plain#3: no description`.
- **`<name>-set`** · only when the widget declares `fields` in `defineWidget`: one typed argument per field
  (`editor-set {"text": "…"}`, `counter-set {"count": 42}`). The set goes to the widget as the built-in command
  `mojoui.set {field, value}`; the widget's setter changes it and the widget emits its own event, so `update()` hears it
  exactly as from a person (the note's word count follows). An undeclared field or a value of the wrong JSON type is
  refused by the agent host, by the runtime (JSON only) and again by the page's runtime (declared fields only).

Widgets run only where there is a web view, so an agent sees them by **attaching** to a running host instead of running
its own session (D-631). Start the host with `MOJOUI_AGENT_SOCKET=<path>` and the agent with `--attach <path>`:
```
MOJOUI_AGENT_SOCKET=/run/user/$UID/widgets.sock pixi run python mojoui/hosts/web.py build/widgets/web   # then open the page
MOJOUI_AGENT_SOCKET=/run/user/$UID/widgets.sock build/widgets/linux/widgets                             # or the GTK app
claude mcp add widgets -- pixi run python mojoui/hosts/agent.py --attach /run/user/$UID/widgets.sock
```
**The agent link** is the host's side: a Unix socket (mode 0600, only when the variable is set), one JSON request per
line, one JSON answer per line. `{"op":"view"}` → `{ok, title, design, nodes, widgets, busy}` (the tree every host
reads, plus what each widget says about itself); `event {node, second, text, number}`, `gesture {node, kind, x, y, dx,
dy, zoom}`, `key {node, name, modifiers}`, `set {tag, id, field, value: JSON text}`, `describe {node, first, count}`,
`rows {node, first, count}`. The web host serves it from web.py for the newest open page and pushes changes to the page
as effects do (`/wait`); the GTK host from its main loop (`mojoui/hosts/agent_link.mojo`, `g_unix_fd_add`). On the web
the widgets report what they show to the server only while an agent is attached (`data-agent` on the page).
Attached, `render` isn't offered (the host draws its own canvases); everything else works as in the agent's own session.

## What an agent gets back from act
What changed, in words: the new texts (`Now: status-bar: Saved kit.omx`), what opened or closed (`Opened: dialog "Settings"`),
a design change, and the tools that appeared or went. Enough to carry on without a second call.

## What it can't do yet
- Attached to a host: `render` (it draws in the agent's own session only), and the Mac's host has no agent link yet.
- Read cells on any app but omxplorer (the others don't `describe` their canvases); omxplorer reads the shown rows, not a range.
- Move Board objects, drag, or scroll a grid by gesture beyond what `pan` sends.
- Generate UI: that is AG-UI, after MX frame (the operations log is its state).

## What it costs in tokens
Measured 2026-10-22 on omxplorer with `build/data/orders_1m.csv`, through `scripts/agent_client.py` (tokens estimated as characters ÷ 4):

| Call | Characters | ≈ Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| `ask` "revenue by product, largest first, top 5" (what changed) | 256 | 60 |
| `read` (the screen's texts) | 916 | 230 |
| `insert-chart` | 1,063 | 270 |
| `create-table`, `choose-a-file` | 2,500–2,600 | 650 |
| `screen` (everything, a busy screen with 100 tools) | 11,393 | 2,800 |
| `tools/list` (104 tools, as JSON) | 17,437 | 4,400 |

For comparison, one screenshot costs a vision model about 1,600 tokens (Claude: width × height ÷ 750, after resizing to about 1.15 megapixels), and a screen-scraping agent takes one after every action to see what happened. So a call that answers in words is 2–25× cheaper than that screenshot; a full `screen` or a fresh tool list is not, and is worth asking for only when the screen changed a lot.


---

<!-- source: docs/ui-threads.md -->

# The UI thread: why apps don't hang, and the rules that keep it that way

An app built on omxcode should never freeze, on any platform, without its author thinking about threads. This page
says how the framework makes that true, the few rules an app (or an agent writing one) follows, what each platform
does today, and how it's checked. The evidence for each claim is in [component-practices.md](component-practices.md)
§1–§2 and the decisions it names.

## The idea in one paragraph

Every platform (GTK, AppKit, UIKit, Android, the browser) draws on **one thread**, the UI thread, and lets nothing
else touch its widgets. At 60 frames a second that thread has about **16 ms per frame** (8 ms at 120 Hz). Anything
that takes longer, like a network call, opening a file or a big query, freezes the window if it runs there. So omxcode
splits every app in two: `update()` and `view()` run on the UI thread and must be quick; **slow work runs on worker
threads, and its answer comes back to `update()` as an ordinary event**. The app's state is only ever touched on the
UI thread, so there are no locks, no races and no "which thread am I on?" in app code.

## What the framework guarantees (you get these for free)

| Guarantee | How | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Widgets are only touched on the UI thread | the platform runs the loop and calls into Mojo; Mojo never runs a loop of its own | every host |
| Network requests never block the screen | `Http.get(...)` queues a request; it runs on a worker thread; the reply arrives as an `Event` | `mojoui/effects.mojo`, goal 33 |
| Timers never block | `App.every()` lists `Every(ms, msg)`; ticks arrive as events | `mojoui/effects.mojo` |
| Data work never blocks | `start_ui_job(...)` runs a query, import or sort on its own thread; when it ends, `App.jobs_message()` reaches `update()` | `mojoui/jobs.mojo`, D-771, D-792 |
| Video and pictures never block | a decoder thread per video (`mojoui/framefeed.mojo`): opening, seeking and decoding run there; the newest seek wins; a frame that lands wakes the UI | goal 41 M2, D-1116 |
| Documents never block | opening a folder, drawing its pages, reading it (OCR) and writing a pack (PDFs, clips) run as jobs (`mojoui/documentjobs.mojo`, `mojoui/pack.mojo`) | goal 41 M10, D-1271 |
| Tables, queries and exports never block | `mojoui/tablejobs.mojo` (Insert > Table, SQL, Export CSV) and `mojoui/videocard.mojo` (Analyze, reels) run as jobs that wake the UI | goal 41 M3–M4, D-1124, D-1131 |
| A finished job shows at once, not a frame later | the job's end wakes the main loop (a pipe on Linux and the web, `performSelectorOnMainThread` on the Mac) | D-771 |
| Cancelling never blocks | cancelling marks the job; checking whether its thread stopped doesn't wait (Linux, Mac) | `mojoui/sheetjobs.mojo` |
| Clicking a button that changes the screen never crashes | rebuilds wait until the click has finished; re-entrant signals are swallowed | every host |
| Big lists don't build big trees | `LazyList` and the data grid draw only what's on screen | D-252 |
| An idle app uses no CPU | canvases tick only while something moves; the web pulls a frame only after the last arrived | D-64, D-57 |

## The rules for an app (and for an agent writing one)

1. **`update()` and `view()` only decide.** They change state and describe the screen. Nothing in them should take
   more than a few milliseconds.
2. **Anything slow is a request, a timer or a job:**

   ```mojo
   # a network call: queue it; the reply comes back to update() as Event(FETCHED, ...)
   self.http.get(FETCHED, "http://localhost:8000/api/orders")

   # data work (a query, an import, a sort): a job; update() hears LANDED when it ends
   self.running = start_ui_job(StepJob(self.orders.value(), self.filters))
   def jobs_message(self) -> Int: return LANDED
   ```

3. **A job owns its inputs.** Hand it a snapshot or a copy (`sheet.snapshot()`), never a reference to the app's
   state; read its result back with `poll()` / `result()` in `update()`.
4. **Draw big things on a canvas, list big things lazily.** Don't build a widget per row.
5. **Never sleep or wait in `update()`.** Use `App.every()` for "later".

Follow these and the app runs without freezing on every platform below. Break rule 1 or 2 and no framework can save
it: SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose and React all share that limit (see "What's next" for how omxcode will catch it).

## Where each platform stands (measured)

| Platform | Requests and timers | Data jobs on their own thread | Finished job wakes the screen | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linux (GTK) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ 0.02–0.05 ms median | `examples/jobwake`: a 1.5 s job, 90 frames while it ran, longest gap 17 ms |
| Web | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | goal 33, D-771 |
| Mac (AppKit) | ✅ | ✅ (D-792) | ✅ ~35 ms median on GitHub's virtual Macs | a 1.5 s job: longest frame gap 1516–1527 ms before → 71–83 ms after, macOS 15 and 26 |
| iPhone (UIKit) | builds, never run | ❌ jobs still run on the main thread | ❌ frame poll only | needs the Mac's fix plus a UIKit wake |
| Android | not checked | threaded build, not measured | frame poll; cancelling a job waits for its thread | runs on the emulator; none of this measured there |

The Mac numbers are from GitHub's virtual Macs (no GPU, ~20 frames a second), with the CPU build. The Mac's GPU
(Metal) build has the same switch but hasn't run with it yet; real-hardware numbers need the owner's MacBook.

## How it's checked

- The watchdog (`MOJOUI_BUDGET_MS=N`, see "What's next" 1) names any update, view or draw over N ms; goal 41's checks
  run omxplorer's sessions at 50 ms on the headless display (CPU drawing) and want no `SLOW:` line.

- `examples/jobwake` measures it: 40 short jobs (how fast a finished job reaches `update()`), then one 1.5 s job and
  the longest time the window went without a frame. It prints **PASS** under 500 ms and **FAIL (the window froze)**
  above, and exits 1 on Linux when it fails. On the Mac it runs on GitHub's runners (`scripts/mac-ci jobwake`).
- Building the Mac app the old way (`MOJOUI_SERIAL_JOBS=1 scripts/build.sh jobwake mac`) shows the freeze it
  prevents: 1 frame in 1.5 s.

## Known edges

- **Deliberate waits, every platform:** replacing a document waits for its cancelled jobs to stop (they may still be
  reading its data). A cancel lands within a block of rows (the engine's claim; not measured here).
- **The Mac's "has the thread stopped?" check reads an engine internal** (the job's reference count, `W_REFS`): the
  engine has no non-blocking `ended()` and Apple has no `pthread_tryjoin_np`. Asked of the engine as request #26
  ([mxframe-needs.md](mxframe-needs.md)); until then an engine change to that order would break it quietly.
- **The Mac's wake is ~35 ms** on GitHub's Macs against 0.05 ms on Linux; unmeasured on real hardware.

- **Python in a job** (goal 41, D-1146): CPython's lock stays with the UI thread, which never lets go on its own. A job
  that calls Python takes the lock with `mojoui.pygil.python_enter()`/`python_exit()`, and whoever starts it lends the
  lock (`python_lend()`, then `python_reclaim()` when the result is taken; mojoui.documentjobs does both). While it is
  lent, Python on the UI thread must go through `python_enter()` too (pdfsource and ocrmodel do; visionmodel doesn't yet).
  Under a Python host (the web host, the agent host: the app is a module Python imported) Python owns the lock and lets
  go between calls; lending there would crash, so `python_lend()` does nothing and a job waits for Python's next pause
  (D-1260). Checked: goal 41 M10's scenario reads 17 BOLs with docTR in a job under the agent host, 0 `SLOW:` at 50 ms.

## What's next, so it's "drop in a component and it just works"

1. **Catch a slow `update()`: done (goal 41 M1).** Run any app with `MOJOUI_BUDGET_MS=16` and, from its first second
   on, every `update()`, `view()` or canvas draw over the budget prints `SLOW: update msg=7 80.06 ms` (the message),
   `SLOW: view msg=7 …` or `SLOW: draw canvas=3 …` (the canvas's tag), so an app author or an agent sees the freeze
   before a user does. The runtime times it (`Runtime.watch`, `mojoui/app.mojo`), so every host gets it: GTK and the
   web (the server's log; `scripts/drive.py` forwards it) are checked by `examples/slowcheck`; AppKit and Android turn
   it on too (unrun; Android's stdout goes nowhere, so read it with `adb logcat` only once stdout is redirected);
   UIKit doesn't read the environment. The next step is a frame budget that names what inside the update was slow.
2. **The iPhone**: the Mac's job threads plus a UIKit wake, checked on the owner's iPhone.
3. **The Mac's GPU build** run with job threads (a job's Metal queries from its own thread), on the owner's MacBook.

## JavaScript widgets (WebComponent)

Each is a `WebComponent` (above) with its own bundle; a cell is the WebComponent's state on that host, ✅ only where a check runs the app that ships the widget. Agent: ✅ where the widget describes itself and the agent's checks drive the app attached to a host (goal 34b M0).

| Widget | Library | Gets | Linux (GTK) | Web | Android | Mac (AppKit) | iPhone (UIKit) | Agent (MCP) | Lives in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mx-counter` | plain JS (vendored) | agent read, agent set, Tab stop | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | 🔨 | ❌ | ✅ | `examples/widgets/web/widgets/counter.js` |
| `mx-chart` | Apache ECharts (echarts 6.1.0) | agent read, theme, Tab stop | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | 🔨 | ❌ | ✅ | `mojoui/widgets/chart.ts` |
| `mx-editor` | CodeMirror 6 (@codemirror/state 6.5.2) | agent read, agent set, theme, Tab stop | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | 🔨 | ❌ | ✅ | `mojoui/widgets/editor.ts` |

## Inside one app, not components yet (the debt)

| Should become | Lives in | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `FormulaBar` | examples/workbook | what's selected, its value, a formula field; migrate to mojoui.sheetchrome.FormulaBar |
| `Inspector` | examples/mxstudio | the side panel: Comes from, Feeds, Your edits, Undo all (lineage and the edit log); migrate to mojoui.inspector |
| `Toolbar / StatusBar islands` | examples/workbook | the island contents (title, Insert buttons, status) are assembled by the app; migrate to mojoui.sheetchrome |
| `Selection totals (sum, average of a column on the GPU)` | examples/omxplorer | the status bar's numbers: a group-by with one group, formatted by the column |
| `Import review (columns, types, empties, first rows)` | examples/omxplorer | the Import step's table; a component once a second app imports files |
| `Chart / pivot inspector sections` | examples/omxplorer | type, value, group by, rows and columns as Inspector sections; belongs beside mojoui.sheetpage |
| `Report toolbar controls (tile column, add-tile tools, filter)` | examples/omxplorer | the column new tiles use, the Sum / Average / Count / Chart tile tools and the filter (column, value), in the Report's toolbar; belongs in mojoui.reportpage |

## The rule

Before building a feature: list the components it needs, mark each ✅ / 🔨 / ❌ here, build or extend the component in `mojoui/` first (its own test, every host it can reach), then build the app from it. An app never draws something another app would need; if it does, it goes in the table above until it's extracted.
